title: Lagos State increases 2026 HIV response budget by 35% in Nigeria | HealthCare Middle East & Africa - No.1 Health & Pharma Manufacturing Industry Publication

contentHtml:
NIGERIA—Lagos State Government has increased its 2026 HIV response budget by 35% to N1.065 billion (US$767,000), from N791 million (US$569,000), to strengthen treatment access and reduce reliance on international funding.

Dr. Folakemi Animashaun, Chief Executive Officer of the Lagos State AIDS Control Agency (LSACA), announced the increase on November 19, during a press briefing at Baguada Kaltho Press Centre in Alausa, Ikeja, to launch activities for the 2026 World AIDS Day.

The agency has also started distributing antiretroviral medicines purchased by the state government to help maintain uninterrupted treatment for people living with HIV.

Animashaun said the increased funding and the local procurement programme reflected the government’s commitment to taking greater responsibility for the state’s HIV response amid changes to international health financing.

Domestic funding and treatment sustainability

To strengthen long-term financing, Lagos State is developing a ten-year HIV Response Transition and Sustainability Roadmap covering 2027 to 2036.

The framework will address domestic financing, healthcare delivery, workforce capacity, medicines, diagnostics, community participation and institutional accountability.

Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu is expected to launch the roadmap at the World AIDS Day Symposium on December 1, alongside the presentation of the state-procured antiretroviral medicines.

Animashaun clarified that increased domestic investment was not intended to replace development partners but to strengthen existing partnerships and protect essential services against fluctuations in external funding.

She also emphasised that reliable medicine supplies would require accurate forecasting, quality assurance, efficient distribution and continuous stock monitoring.

“The true measure of treatment security is not simply the purchase of medicines; it is whether the person who needs those medicines can obtain them consistently, without interruption,” she said.

HIV testing and treatment access

LSACA’s consolidated programme records showed 387,558 HIV-negative test results and 7,584 HIV-positive results.

Animashaun cautioned that these figures represented test results rather than new infections or necessarily unique individuals tested.

The agency also recorded 156,122 new antenatal care clients, alongside 156,109 HIV-negative test results among pregnant and breastfeeding women, highlighting the role of integrated HIV and maternal healthcare services.

Between January and October 2026, community-based programmes conducted 25,167 HIV tests among people aged 15 and above, recording 1,166 positive results.

Animashaun said the agency was prioritising linkage to treatment, continuity of care and patient support alongside testing and diagnosis.

She identified stigma, discrimination, financial constraints and limited access to services as barriers that continued to discourage residents from seeking HIV prevention and treatment.

She urged residents to access prevention services, including condoms, HIV testing, pre-exposure prophylaxis and post-exposure prophylaxis where medically indicated.

 She also highlighted the Undetectable Equals Untransmittable principle, which confirms that people who maintain an undetectable viral load through effective treatment do not transmit HIV sexually.

World AIDS Day activities

This year’s commemoration runs under the theme “Ending AIDS Starts with Access: Equity, Ownership, and Sustainability.”

Activities began on November 19 with a press briefing and awareness rally, followed by a novelty football match at Campos Stadium on November 21.

Other events include an empowerment programme for people living with HIV on November 23, a Jumat service on November 27, and a church service on November 29.

The programme will culminate in a symposium at Balmoral Event Centre in Lagos on December 1, bringing together government officials, development partners, healthcare professionals and community representatives.

Animashaun also acknowledged the contributions of UNAIDS, the United States Health Assistance Office and the Global Fund, calling for continued cooperation to sustain HIV prevention, testing and treatment services.
